lectures.title: Why we are not learning iptables

cues.en: In this lecture, I want to preemptively answer the question Why don't we learn IP tables here in this
course?
Because I feel like IP tables, it's such a common term that if I don't talk about it, people might.
Or you might wonder why do we learn firewalld here and not IP tables?
IP tables is a userspace program that allows us to configure the netfilter of the kernel.
So we got the kernel subsystem.
The Netfilter subsystem and IP tables is a program that runs outside of our kernel and it's used to
configure this kernel subsystem so that it does what we want.
So for example, we want to block certain ports or we want to allow certain ports and so on.
So what's the problem here?
This is what we want to do.
Well, technically that's true.
The IP tables is not yet deprecated, at least as of recording this course.
So that means IP tables is supported software that we can use to set up our firewall rules.
This is totally all right.
However, this is what the IP tables maintainers say.
Let's have a look at what Red Hat Enterprise Linux says about IP tables.
They say in their documentation that the IP set and IP tables and packages have been deprecated in Red
Hat, Enterprise Linux and the IP tables.
NFT package contains different tools for example, the IP tables command.
So this means even though the IP tables command itself as a standalone project, it's not deprecated.
IPTables on CentOS and on Red Hat Enterprise Linux is indeed deprecated.
So that means that Red Hat Enterprise Linux and by them also for example, CentOS and also Fedora,
of course they are all moving away from using iptables and they are saying now on those operating systems
using iptables is still supported but it's deprecated and we should no longer use it for new installations
and new systems that we set up.
Also for example, in the Gentoo Linux documentation, that's another Linux distribution we haven't
looked at here in the course, but they for example, say that iptables should be replaced with, with
its successor, Nftables, which is another tool that allows us to configure our firewall.
Gentoo Linux is a Linux distribution that's popular for people that want to build their whole system
from source code.
So there the package management that we usually would not download binary packages on a Gentoo Linux,
but we would download the source code and compile it manually and Gentoo Linux is optimized for that.
So it's actually for learning Linux.
Quite a I could quite recommend using that for a while.
If you do have spare time and you do have time to go through additional problems that come from that,
but it will help you get a bigger or a deep understanding of Linux.
I personally used it when I was younger quite a bit.
So but anyway, in their documentation, for example, they say that it should be replaced with its
successor Nftables for ubuntu and Debian.
I couldn't find anything like this, but I would assume that now if more and more distributions are
moving away or migrating away from iptables at some point also those distributions will follow.
So the question is why is iptables in the process of being deprecated?
Well, the first thing is that it has quite a complex syntax, so it's definitely not easy to use.
It's less performant.
So if we change a rule, the whole rules from the kernel need to be transmitted to our IPTables program.
Then we change the rule and we write all the rules back to our kernel.
So it has quite a bit of overhead because we can't just change a single rule and send this as a message
to our kernel.
We need to update a single rule in a sense that we get everything from our kernel, do our changes and
put it back into our kernel so it's less performant, which because of this lack of atomic rule set
updates, this is what causes this performance issue.
And we also have different tools, for example for IPV four and IPV six.
So for example, we have the IPTables command or the IPV six tables from command for IPV six.
So this also makes it a little bit convenient.
And I would say this is my feeling right now that it's in the process of being deprecated from Linux
distributions.
So the first ones have started as we've seen with Red Hat, Enterprise Linux.
And my speculation would be that also others will follow my suggestion or my feeling is that I would
like to make a bold statement here.
I know it's a little bit bold for now, but I would say that if you're not trying to pass a Linux exam
that requires knowledge and IP tables or you're not working with systems that still use IP tables,
there's not really a reason to learn IP tables nowadays.
So I would say especially the first one, but also probably the second, they are valid reasons here.
But aside from that, I would not recommend you learning IP tables.
Please be aware though that I'm making quite a bold statement here that is also maybe a little bit opinionated,
but I would say let's now get started with Firewalld and how that works.
And in the next lecture we will have a look at the architecture of Firewalld.
